title: Cosmic Geography: When Height Becomes a Claim About Heaven
introduction: In Obadiah we have a dwelling set inside a rock that is up high. That is to say: hidden and elevated at the same time. Edom possesses two forms of security simultaneously, vertical inaccessibility: I am too high for you to reach me, and horizontal inaccessibility: I am hidden inside the rock so that you cannot find me. As Obadiah 3 says: "The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high, who says in his heart, ‘Who will bring me down to the ground?’"
finalWord: God judges Edom without turning ‘being a descendant of Edom’ into an irreversible moral condition. The sentence against Edom does not turn Edomite blood into sin. God judges a historical house, a kingdom, a national structure marked by a particular rebellion. That means that centuries later a person of Idumean ancestry is still a real moral agent. But it also tells us that God’s grace reaches everyone alike.

points.title: When Height Becomes a Claim About Heaven
points.text:
That means that in the process of thought, hidden equals elevated equals cosmically unreachable. Now, this raises another spiritual question: the farther out of human reach Edom believes itself to be, the closer to heaven it imagines itself to be.

In the biblical world, ‘the stars’ are not only points of light. They can belong to the language of the heavenly realm. For example, Job 38:7 places the morning stars alongside the sons of God: ‘when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy.’ Other texts speak of the host of heaven. This is the language Obadiah 4 picks up: ‘Though you mount on high as the eagle, and though your nest is set among the stars, I will bring you down from there,’ says Yahweh.

For an ancient reader, moving poetically from the mountains up to a nest ‘among the stars’ means having already left normal topography behind and having entered cosmic language. And there Obadiah is possibly saying something bigger than ‘Edom thinks its mountains are high.’ His expression could be deeper: ‘Edom has turned a geographical advantage into a cosmic claim.’ Edom believes it stands in the same realm, on the same level, as the gods.

points.title: Motivated Reasoning: Pride Does Not Invent Facts, It Recruits Them
points.text:
‘The pride of your heart has deceived you’ (Obadiah 3). Edom does not control the mechanism that holds up its confidence. It moves illegitimately from ‘this is hard to conquer’ to ‘nobody can bring me down.’

There is an enormous difference between ‘this is hard to conquer’ and ‘no one will be able to bring me down.’ These are different ways in which sin distorts our understanding of reality.

The problem is not first of all in the information Edom possesses. The problem is in the instrument with which it interprets that information. The rock is real. The height is real. The military difficulty is real. The proud heart interprets a fact correctly and then illegitimately draws an absolute conclusion from it. Edom is deceived about what the rock means.

Pride does not need to manufacture false data. Very often it works with true data badly interpreted. Self deception normally begins with a partial truth that the heart stretches beyond what that truth can guarantee. That is to say, the sin of pride does not eliminate reason, it recruits it.

Motivated reasoning. First I want something to be true. Then I begin to select the data that make it plausible that it is true. And finally I forget that it was I who selected the data.

points.title: ‘I Have Made You Small’: The Shape of the Judgment and the History That Follows
points.text:
‘I have made you small’ in the Hebrew perfect tense: is this a sentence already settled in the divine purpose (Cambridge), or a prior territorial condition that should have restrained Edom’s pride (Calvin)? The first reading has better immediate coherence. Obadiah 2 reads: ‘Behold, I have made you small among the nations. You are greatly despised.’

Did God sovereignly make Edom a small nation precisely because of the arrogance and the pride that were in its spirit?

Pride is an argument with God about the size we really are. That is exactly what is happening here.

THE FORM OF THE JUDGMENT

Now, on this point, God does not begin by saying to Edom: ‘I will destroy you.’ He says first: ‘I will make you small.’ Because the judgment corresponds to the disease. This is the law of retaliation and proportionality applied.

‘I will make you small’ is corrective in the form of the judgment, but Obadiah does not present the judgment as therapeutic or restorative for Edom.

The judgment is epistemologically corrective (in its verbal and nominal form), but judicially retributive (proportional to the reality of the sin).

FROM EDOM TO IDUMEA

The Iron Age kingdom of Edom was basically southeast of the Dead Sea, in what today would be Jordan. Over the centuries, Edomite populations gradually moved westward. In the Hellenistic period that region came to be known as Idumea, the Greco Roman form related to Edom, and its inhabitants as Idumeans.

At the end of the second century B.C., the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea. Josephus recounts that he allowed the Idumeans to remain there on the condition that they be circumcised and adopt the Jewish laws. According to his account, from that point on they were incorporated into the Jewish people.

And out of that comes one of the most famous figures in the New Testament: Herod the Great.

His father, Antipater, was an Idumean. Josephus identifies him explicitly in this way, and the ancient sources even record that Herod’s opponents reproached him for his Idumean origin.

Mark 3:7 and 8 tells us that crowds began to come to Jesus from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, and also from Idumea: ‘Jesus withdrew to the sea with his disciples; and a great multitude followed him from Galilee, from Judea, from Jerusalem, from Idumaea, beyond the Jordan, and those from around Tyre and Sidon. A great multitude, hearing what great things he did, came to him.’

Mark says that a great multitude coming from Idumea and from other regions heard what Jesus was doing and came to him.
